summary: This informational RFC describes a procedure where a military message is composed by one user and released only once Authorizing Users approve by adding the MMHS-Authorizing-Users header field. The result can be signed by sender and reviewer.

plainLanguage.summary: A message sits in drafts until a supervisor approves it by adding their name to the header.

questions: how does email message approval work
how can i verify message authorization
what is the draft and release procedure
subtitle: A header field for military message approval and secure release

tldr.problem: In secure military environments, email messages cannot be released until one or more authorized officers approve them, but there was no standard way to track and enforce this approval.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7912 adds the MMHS-Authorizing-Users header field to email. Before a message is sent, Authorizing Users review and add their email addresses to this header, optionally signing it with S/MIME to prove they authorized release.
tldr.outcome: Recipients can verify that the message was reviewed and approved by authorized personnel, and the original sender's signature (if any) remains intact alongside the authorization signatures.

today: RFC 7912 is an Informational RFC and remains the specification for implementing draft and release procedures in email systems that require authorization before message delivery. It is not an Internet Standard but is widely used in military and government messaging systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Some organizations, especially military and government agencies, require email messages to be reviewed and authorized before they are delivered. RFC 7912 describes how to implement this draft and release procedure using a standard header field.

The core idea is simple: a message composed by a drafter (the original sender) stays in draft status until one or more Authorizing Users (such as releasing officers) review it and add their email addresses to a new header field called MMHS-Authorizing-Users. Only then does the message get released to the message transfer system for delivery to recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like a letter that sits on a manager's desk until they sign off on it.

sections.title: The Draft and Release Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure has several steps. First, a drafter composes a message and optionally signs it with S/MIME. The message is submitted to the Message Submission Agent (MSA), which forwards it to one or more Authorizing Users (determined by domain configuration). The MSA MUST validate that the MMHS-Authorizing-Users header field, if present, contains valid addresses and matches any review signatures.

Each Authorizing User then reviews the message for content and correctness. The UA (user agent) verifies the drafter's signature if present. The Authorizing User checks whether they have already approved it (to prevent loops). If approved, they can add their email address to the MMHS-Authorizing-Users header and optionally add an S/MIME review signature. The updated message is then either released to the message transfer system or passed to another Authorizing User for additional approval.
sections.plainLanguage: Each approver reads the message, checks that it came from who it says it did, and adds their name to the approval list before sending it onward.

sections.title: The MMHS-Authorizing-Users Header Field
sections.content:
The MMHS-Authorizing-Users header field is simple: it contains a comma-separated list of email addresses representing the users or entities that authorized the message. The header MUST NOT appear more than once in a message. If multiple copies are found, the message is malformed and agents SHOULD either bounce it or fix it to contain only one copy.

The header field has this format:

MMHS-Authorizing-Users: user1@domain.com, user2@domain.com

In some environments, a group address may be used instead of individual names if the organization requires that the identities of authorizers remain hidden from recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is just a list of names of the people who said the message is okay to send.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious sender could try to forge an MMHS-Authorizing-Users header to bypass the authorization process. For this reason, agents and clients MUST verify that the header is authentic by checking for a corresponding S/MIME review signature or DKIM signature that proves a particular person actually authorized the message. Without signature protection, the header alone cannot be trusted.

Implementations MUST be robust against malformed headers. An attacker could submit an extraordinarily large or otherwise malformed MMHS-Authorizing-Users header to try to exploit parsing code. Agents receiving messages from MTAs must validate the header thoroughly.

For environments where identities must be hidden, organizations can use group email addresses in the header, so recipients know the message was approved by someone in that group without learning who it was.
sections.plainLanguage: If you just trust the approval header without checking the signature, a bad actor could fake it. You have to make sure someone actually signed it to prove they authorized it.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: RFC 7912 registers the MMHS-Authorizing-Users header field with IANA in the Provisional Message Header Field Names registry. The registration documents the field name, its applicable protocol (email under RFC 5322), and a reference to this RFC. This ensures that the header name is officially recognized and prevents conflicts with other uses.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA officially recorded that this header name exists and what it is used for.
